question: A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after he was involved in a motorcycle collision. He was not wearing a helmet. Physical examination shows left periorbital ecchymosis. A CT scan of the head shows a fracture of the greater wing of the left sphenoid bone with compression of the left superior orbital fissure. Physical examination of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?

enhanced_information: In the case of a fracture of the greater wing of the left sphenoid bone with compression of the left superior orbital fissure, the cranial nerves most likely affected are III, IV, V1, and VI. This can lead to ophthalmoplegia, which includes impaired eye movements and potentially an absent corneal reflex due to involvement of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (V1). Therefore, numbness of the left cheek is unlikely as it involves the maxillary branch (V2), which is not affected in this scenario. Preserved left lateral gaze is unlikely due to potential impairment of the abducens nerve (VI), which controls lateral eye movement. Complete loss of vision is unlikely as the optic nerve (II) is not typically involved in superior orbital fissure syndrome. Decreased sense of smell is also unlikely as the olfactory nerve (I) is not involved. The most likely finding is an absent left corneal reflex due to V1 involvement.
analysis: The patient has a fracture of the greater wing of the left sphenoid bone with compression of the left superior orbital fissure. The superior orbital fissure syndrome, also known as Rochon-Duvigneaud's syndrome, involves damage to the structures passing through the superior orbital fissure. These structures include cranial nerves III (oculomotor), IV (trochlear), V1 (ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve), and VI (abducens). Damage to these nerves can lead to ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, and sensory loss in the distribution of the ophthalmic nerve. The numbness of the left cheek is associated with the maxillary branch (V2) of the trigeminal nerve, which is not affected in superior orbital fissure syndrome. Therefore, the most likely finding in this patient would be ophthalmoplegia, which would include the inability to perform certain eye movements, such as lateral gaze. However, since the question asks for a specific finding, 'Preserved left lateral gaze' would not be correct, as lateral gaze would be affected. The most likely correct answer is 'Absent left corneal reflex,' as this involves the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (V1), which is affected in superior orbital fissure syndrome.
